chapter_title: Post-Processing Stack V2 - Setup & Basic Effects
chapter_summary:
Post-processing refers to a collection of full-screen image effects that are applied to a camera's rendered image *after* the main scene rendering has completed, but *before* the image is displayed on screen. These effects are crucial for achieving a cinematic look, establishing mood, and adding a layer of polish that significantly elevates the visual quality of your 3D art. Think of it as the final touch-up in photography or film production – adjusting colors, adding glows, blurring backgrounds, or simulating camera lens imperfections. Without post-processing, even a beautifully modeled and lit scene can appear flat and uninspiring. With it, you can transform a generic scene into something vibrant, moody, realistic, or stylized.

To utilize post-processing in Unity, you'll typically use the **Post-Processing Stack V2** package. Like VFX Graph, this package is designed to work optimally with Unity's Scriptable Render Pipelines (URP or HDRP). If you're not using an SRP, you might need to use an older version of the Post-Processing Stack or alternative solutions. Installation is done via the Package Manager (Window > Package Manager), searching for and installing "Post Processing." Once installed, there are three main components you'll interact with: the `Post-Process Layer` on your camera, the `Post-Process Volume` in your scene, and `Post-Process Profile` assets.

First, your main camera needs to know it should process post-processing effects. Select your camera and add a `Post-Process Layer` component to it. This component requires you to set a `Layer` mask. It's good practice to create a dedicated layer for post-processing (e.g., "PostProcessing") and assign it here. This layer doesn't need to contain any objects; it simply acts as a filter for the camera. Next, you need to define *where* and *how* post-processing effects are applied. This is done using a **Post-Process Volume**. Create an empty GameObject (or a simple cube) and add a `Post-Process Volume` component to it. Crucially, this GameObject must be on the same layer you assigned in your camera's `Post-Process Layer` component (e.g., "PostProcessing").

The `Post-Process Volume` component has a `Is Global` checkbox. If checked, the effects defined in this volume will apply to the entire scene, regardless of the camera's position. If unchecked, the volume acts as a local trigger: effects will only apply when the camera enters its bounds, and you can blend between different volumes. For most artists, a global volume is a good starting point for overall scene mood. The volume also requires a **Profile** asset. This is where you actually enable and configure individual post-processing effects. Create a new Post-Process Profile (Assets > Create > Post-Process Profile) and drag it into the `Profile` slot of your `Post-Process Volume`. Now, within this profile, you can add effects.

Let's explore some fundamental effects:
*   **Bloom:** This effect adds a soft glow around bright areas of your scene, simulating the way light bleeds onto a camera sensor or film. It's excellent for enhancing emissive materials, light sources, or creating a dreamy, ethereal look. You can adjust its `Intensity`, `Threshold` (how bright an area needs to be to bloom), and `Scatter`. A common mistake is over-doing Bloom, making the scene look washed out; use it subtly.
*   **Vignette:** This darkens the edges of the screen, drawing the viewer's eye towards the center. It's a classic cinematic effect used to add depth, focus, or a sense of age/nostalgia. You can control its `Intensity`, `Smoothness`, and `Color`.
*   **Color Grading:** Perhaps the most powerful effect for artists, Color Grading allows you to remap and adjust the colors of your scene, fundamentally changing its mood and aesthetic. You can tweak `Temperature` (warm/cool), `Tint` (green/magenta), `Exposure`, `Contrast`, `Saturation`, and even use `Color Wheels` for fine-tuning shadows, midtones, and highlights. This is where you can achieve looks ranging from gritty realism to vibrant fantasy.

When working with post-processing, remember that each effect adds to the rendering cost. While modern GPUs handle these effects efficiently, it's a good safety note to enable only the effects you truly need and to optimize their settings. Start with conservative values and gradually increase them until you achieve the desired visual impact without significant performance degradation. Post-processing is an iterative process; experiment with combinations of effects and their settings to discover unique visual styles for your 3D art.

narration.text: Post-processing is the final polish you apply to a camera image after the scene renders but before it appears on screen. In this chapter you will learn what post-processing is, how to install Unity’s Post-Processing Stack V2, and how to wire the Post-Process Layer, Volume, and Profile together so effects actually appear. We’ll focus on three practical effects: Bloom to add soft glows around bright features, Vignette to guide the viewer’s eye by darkening edges, and Color Grading to set mood through temperature, contrast, and saturation. You will see specific inspector values to try, a recommended global volume setup for quick iteration, and a short troubleshooting checklist for when effects don’t show up. Along the way I’ll explain why each step matters: the layer mask tells the camera which volumes to process, the profile stores effect parameters, and global volumes let you shape the whole scene quickly. By the end you’ll be able to create a subtle cinematic look without overdoing effects or introducing obvious performance problems. Keep an eye on intensity sliders and start conservative. To begin, we’ll map the steps and objectives so you know what to practice.

narration.text: We start by defining post-processing and why it matters for 3D art. Post-processing is a set of full-screen image effects applied after the scene renders but before display. This final pass controls how light blooms, how the edges fall off, and how colors map across shadows and highlights. Understanding this lets you shape mood and direct attention even when your geometry and lighting are already solid. Next, you will learn how to install the Post-Processing Stack V2 via Unity’s Package Manager. This step is practical: without the package, the inspector components and profile asset options are not available. Finally, you will practice adding the Post-Process Layer to your camera and creating a dedicated layer mask. That mask is a small but crucial piece — it tells the camera which volumes to apply and prevents accidental processing when you have multiple cameras or editor-only volumes. Each objective includes a brief practice cue so you can verify competency in the editor. By the end of this screen you’ll be able to explain post-processing, install the official package, and recognize the camera component that enables the system.

screens.title: What is Post-Processing?
screens.subtitle: A clear definition and why it changes your final image

narration.text: Post-processing is a collection of full-screen effects applied to an image after the scene finishes rendering but before the image displays on screen. This placement is important: it means post-processing works on the final composed image, not on individual materials or meshes. Think of it like a photographer’s final color correction and lens choices applied to a frame. You can add glows, simulate lens artifacts, darken edges, or globally remap color. These effects are essential because they unify otherwise disparate visual elements—lighting, textures, and emissive materials—and give the player a consistent, intentional mood. A concrete example: if you have emissive neon lights in a scene, enabling Bloom makes the neon appear to glow beyond the geometry and blend naturally into the frame. A common misconception is to treat post-processing as an optional ornament; while subtle effects are ornaments, many scenes rely on a small amount of post-processing to read correctly on different screens. Another misconception is applying extreme values early; instead, start conservative and iterate. Key takeaway: post-processing is the final, global step to shape mood and focus. Ask yourself when tuning: does this effect guide the viewer or distract them?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Full-screen image effects applied after rendering that alter the final look to create mood, focus, and cinematic polish.

content.html:
Core Concept What is Post-Processing?

Post-processing defined

Full-screen corrections applied after rendering to adjust glow, color, and lens effects across the whole image.

Analogy & Example

Imagine finishing a photo and adding a soft glow to highlights and a slight vignette to draw attention. In Unity, Bloom and Vignette do that for a camera’s image. For example, neon signs with emissive materials look more believable when Bloom is applied; the light bleeds beyond the mesh edges just like a camera sensor would capture it.

Common misconception

Don’t assume stronger values equal better visuals. Excessive Bloom or heavy grading often washes out detail. Start small, iterate, and check the scene at multiple exposures.

Key Takeaway

Post-processing is a subtle but powerful last step. Use it to unify lighting and direct attention without overpowering detail.

Quick comparison
Before
Flat highlights, no sensor glow, edges crisp to the frame.
After
Subtle glow, softened highlights, focused center using vignette.
Try this
Enable a minimal Bloom and Vignette and toggle them to compare. Notice how mood and readability change more than geometry.

screens.title: Install the Post-Processing Package
screens.subtitle: Add the official package so inspector components and profiles become available

narration.text: Installing the Post-Processing Stack V2 is a quick but necessary step. Open the Package Manager from the Window menu, search for "Post Processing," and install the package. If your project uses the Scriptable Render Pipeline—URP or HDRP—this package integrates well and exposes the necessary components. If you are not using an SRP, be aware that behavior differs and you may need alternative solutions. After installing, look in the Inspector for the Post-Process Layer component and the ability to create Post-Process Profile assets. A typical gotcha is forgetting to restart the editor or reselect the camera so the new component options appear correctly in the Add Component menu. A concrete example: after installation, create a new Post-Process Profile via Assets > Create > Post-Process Profile and add it to a Post-Process Volume to confirm installation. Misconception alert: installing the package does not automatically enable effects—components must be added to the camera and volume. Closing takeaway: installation provides the tools, but wiring the camera, volume, and profile is what makes effects visible. Install the Post-Processing Package means use window > package manager to add the post-processing package; then create a post-process profile to confirm the install.. In practical terms, add the official package so inspector components and profiles become available. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Install Package
keyIdea.text: Use Window > Package Manager to add the Post-Processing package; then create a Post-Process Profile to confirm the install.

content.html:
Process Install Package

Install via Package Manager

Step-by-step
  1. Open Window > Package Manager.
  2. Search for "Post Processing" and choose the official package.
  3. Click Install and wait for completion.
  4. Create a Profile: Assets > Create > Post-Process Profile.
  5. Confirm Add Component shows Post-Process Layer on camera.
Quick verification

Create a profile, add a small Bloom effect, and attach the profile to a volume to ensure the install works and the menu shows new components.

Editor tip

If the component options don’t appear, try reselecting the camera or restarting the editor. The package exposes Inspector components that must be added manually.

Key Takeaway

Installation unlocks components and assets, but you must wire the camera and volume to see effects.

screens.title: Add a Post-Process Layer to the Camera
screens.subtitle: Layer masks connect the camera to volumes so effects apply correctly

narration.text: The Post-Process Layer is the camera-side component that tells Unity which post-process volumes the camera should sample. Add the Post-Process Layer component to your Main Camera and then set the Layer mask to a dedicated layer, for example "PostProcessing". Creating and assigning a dedicated layer is good practice: it prevents accidental interactions when multiple cameras or editor-only volumes exist. The Layer mask does not require objects to be present on that layer; it simply filters volumes the camera considers. A concrete example: if your volume GameObject is on layer PostProcessing and the camera’s Post-Process Layer mask includes that layer, the camera will apply that volume’s profile. A common mistake is mismatched layers — if the camera mask and the volume’s GameObject layer differ, no effects will appear even if the profile contains enabled effects. Validation steps: after adding the component, open the Post-Process Layer dropdown in the Inspector, confirm the mask includes your chosen layer, and then play the scene to confirm the profile effect is visible. Keep values conservative when you first test so you can see subtle changes.

keyIdea.title: Camera Layer Mask
keyIdea.text: Attach Post-Process Layer to the camera and select a dedicated layer mask so the camera can sample matching volumes.

content.html:
Process Post-Process Layer

Add Post-Process Layer to your Camera

Why the layer mask matters

The layer mask defines which volumes the camera will process. Create a "PostProcessing" layer and assign your volume GameObjects to it so the camera recognizes them reliably.

  • Create layer: Layers > Add Layer...
  • Select Main Camera > Add Component > Post-Process Layer
  • Set Layer mask to your dedicated layer
Common mistake

If layers don’t match between camera and volume, effects won’t show even if the profile is correct.

Validation example

Create a PostProcessGlobalVolume on the PostProcessing layer, link a profile with Bloom enabled, and play the scene. If no change appears, recheck the camera mask.

Pro tip

Use one dedicated layer per post-processing workflow so multiple cameras or split-screen setups remain predictable.

screens.title: Create a Post-Process Volume
screens.subtitle: Global vs local volumes and how profiles are attached

narration.text: A Post-Process Volume defines where effects apply and which Profile stores the effect settings. Create an empty GameObject named "PostProcessGlobalVolume" and assign it to the same dedicated layer you used on the camera. Add a Post-Process Volume component and check Is Global to apply its Profile everywhere. If Is Global is unchecked, the volume becomes local: the camera only applies the effects when inside the GameObject’s bounds and blends between overlapping volumes. Local volumes are powerful for transition areas, interior/exterior blends, or region-specific looks. The Profile asset holds enabled effects and their override values. To attach a Profile, create it in the Project window via Assets > Create > Post-Process Profile and drag it into the Profile slot on your volume. A helpful practice: set up a global volume first for overall mood, then add local volumes for scene transitions or interior color shifts. Misconception check: the GameObject’s layer must match the camera mask. If your effects still don’t show, verify the Profile has enabled override properties. The takeaway: Volumes and Profiles are the scene-side pair that let you store and scope effect settings.

keyIdea.title: Volume & Profile
keyIdea.text: Create a Post-Process Volume, choose global or local behavior, and link a Post-Process Profile asset that contains enabled effect overrides.

content.html:
Process Post-Process Volume

Create and scope a Post-Process Volume

Global vs Local

Global volumes apply everywhere when Is Global is checked. Local volumes apply only inside bounds and can blend with others for smooth transitions.

  • Create empty GameObject > Add Post-Process Volume.
  • Assign the GameObject to the PostProcessing layer.
  • Check or uncheck Is Global depending on scope.
Attach a Profile

Create a Post-Process Profile asset and drag it to the Profile slot of your volume. The profile stores effect overrides, not the volume itself.

Example workflow

Start with a global volume set to a neutral mood. Then add local volumes at doorways or tunnels to subtly change color grading during transitions.

Key Takeaway

Volumes scope effect application; profiles store the adjustable effect values you will tune for mood and clarity.

screens.title: Bloom — Make bright areas glow
screens.subtitle: How Bloom simulates light bleeding and how to tune it

narration.text: Bloom simulates how very bright areas appear to bleed into surrounding pixels on a camera sensor. This produces a soft glow around emissive materials, bright lights, and specular highlights. It’s most useful for making neon, emissive shaders, and high-dynamic highlights feel organic. Key properties you will tune are Intensity, which controls the strength of the glow; Threshold, which decides how bright a pixel must be before it blooms; and Scatter, which changes the size and softness of the glow. A practical starting example from the chapter recommends Intensity around 0.5 and Threshold near 1.05. Try these conservative values first and increase slowly. A common mistake is pushing Intensity too high, which flattens contrast and washes out detail. Another practical tip: combine Bloom with exposure or color grading carefully because both will interact; increasing exposure makes more pixels exceed the Bloom threshold. When testing, toggle Bloom on and off and compare the difference on emissive surfaces—this contrast will show whether the effect supports your intended mood or overpowers the scene. The takeaway: Bloom is subtle augmentation, not a replacement for good lighting.

keyIdea.title: Bloom basics
keyIdea.text: Use Bloom to add glow to bright areas; tune Intensity and Threshold, start conservative, and avoid washing out contrast.

content.html:
Definition Bloom

Bloom: glow from bright pixels

Key controls
  • Intensity: overall glow strength. Start at 0.5.
  • Threshold: how bright a pixel must be to bloom. Try ~1.05.
  • Scatter: bloom spread and softness.
Example

Set Intensity to 0.5 and Threshold to 1.05 on a scene with emissive neon. Toggle to compare the glow effect on and off.

Common mistakes
  • Pushing intensity too far and losing contrast.
  • Not accounting for exposure changes that affect threshold.
Try this

Increase intensity in small steps while observing highlights and midtones. If highlights clip, reduce intensity or raise threshold.

Key Takeaway

Bloom adds cinematic glow when used subtly; tune threshold and intensity together to avoid washed-out images.

screens.title: Vignette — Focus the Frame
screens.subtitle: How Vignette guides the viewer and how to adjust its parameters

narration.text: Vignette darkens or colors the edges of the screen to direct attention toward the center. It’s a classic cinematic tool used to add depth, focus, or an aged film look. Important controls include Intensity, which sets how dark the edges become, Smoothness which controls the feather between edge and center, and Color which can tint the vignette for stylistic effect. A practical approach is to use low intensities—around 0.2 to 0.4—to subtly guide attention without feeling like a frame. A common misconception is that strong vignettes are always cinematic; in many cases they feel like an artifact when applied too aggressively. Use vignette to support composition and not to hide poor lighting. An example scenario: in an indoor scene with the subject centered, a subtle vignette can help keep the eye on the subject when peripheral details distract. When combined with color grading, be mindful that a colored vignette interacts with overall tone; use small amounts and test on different exposure levels. The takeaway: vignette is a compositional aid, not a justification to ignore scene layout. Vignette — Focus the Frame means use vignette to darken or tint edges, guiding attention. start with low intensity and adjust smoothness for a natural falloff.. In practical terms, how vignette guides the viewer and how to adjust its parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Vignette basics
keyIdea.text: Use Vignette to darken or tint edges, guiding attention. Start with low intensity and adjust smoothness for a natural falloff.

content.html:
Definition Vignette

Vignette: drawing the eye

Parameters to know
  • Intensity: darkness of the edges, start 0.2–0.4.
  • Smoothness: feather quality between center and edge.
  • Color: tint the vignette for mood.
Example

Use a slightly warm tint and Intensity 0.3 on a photo-real interior to gently focus the view on the center object.

Misconception

A heavy vignette does not equal cinematic; it often hides framing problems. Use it to support composition, not to fix it.

Try this

Apply a vignette, play the scene, and toggle to compare. Reduce intensity until the viewer’s attention remains but edges don’t feel artificially dark.

Key Takeaway

Vignette is a subtle tool to guide attention. Use low intensities and test across brightness ranges to ensure natural results.

screens.title: Color Grading — Shape mood with color
screens.subtitle: Temperature, Contrast, Saturation, and color wheels

narration.text: Color Grading remaps and adjusts scene colors to establish a mood. It provides controls like Temperature to shift warm or cool tonality, Tint for green versus magenta balance, Exposure and Contrast for dynamic range, and Saturation for color intensity. Advanced controls include color wheels for shadows, midtones, and highlights allowing differential adjustment. A practical starting point is a small temperature shift (for example slightly cool at -10), a modest contrast increase (for example around +15), and conservative saturation adjustments. An example in the chapter instructs setting Temperature slightly cooler and Contrast slightly higher to produce a crisp look. A common misconception is to treat grading as a single-step fix; grading interacts with lighting, exposure, and Bloom. If you boost contrast aggressively, highlights may clip and Bloom will react differently because more pixels exceed the Burst threshold. To validate, toggle grading on and off and compare skin tones, shadow detail, and highlights. The takeaway: use Color Grading to unify palette and atmosphere; test on target displays and iterate in small increments to retain natural detail. Color Grading — Shape mood with color means use temperature, contrast, and color wheels to set mood; adjust in small steps and validate across different brightness levels.. In practical terms, temperature, contrast, saturation, and color wheels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Color Grading essentials
keyIdea.text: Use temperature, contrast, and color wheels to set mood; adjust in small steps and validate across different brightness levels.

content.html:
Core Concept Color Grading

Practical grading controls

Controls to try
  • Temperature: warm/cool shifts. Try -10 for slightly cooler tones.
  • Contrast: increases midtone separation. Try +15 to refine clarity.
  • Saturation: adjust overall color intensity modestly.
Example profile snippet
// Example inspector starting values
Temperature: -10
Contrast: +15
Saturation: 0
Color Wheels

Use separate adjustments for shadows, midtones, and highlights to keep skin tones natural while altering scene ambiance.

Misconception

Avoid extreme global shifts to fix a single issue. Instead isolate changes to highlights or shadows via color wheels when necessary.

Key Takeaway

Color Grading is powerful; use small incremental changes and verify on multiple scenes to avoid unintended clipping or color shifts.

screens.title: Performance and Optimization
screens.subtitle: Balancing visual quality with runtime cost

narration.text: Post-processing effects have a rendering cost. Bloom, complex grading, and certain blur passes can add G P U work, so use only effects you need and optimize their quality settings. The practical rule from the chapter is to start with conservative settings and enable only required effects. For example, if bloom is applied only to a few emissive elements, keep Intensity low and reduce sample counts if the engine exposes them. If using Color Grading in High Definition Range mode, be mindful that processing HDR data can be more expensive than simple LDR remaps. A common optimization is to lower resolution or sample count for costly passes, or to restrict heavy effects to local volumes where they’re most noticeable rather than globally. Concrete example: use a global subtle Color Grading that affects the whole scene, but reserve high-cost bloom or lens dirt for close-up sequences or cutscenes. Misconception: modern GPUs can handle everything—this is false on lower-end hardware and consoles. Always profile and test on target devices. The takeaway: measure impact, enable only necessary effects, and prefer conservative defaults while iterating toward the final look.

keyIdea.title: Optimize effects
keyIdea.text: Enable only needed effects, prefer conservative values, and profile on target hardware to balance quality and performance.

content.html:
Comparison Performance vs Quality

Balance visual fidelity with cost

High Quality (costly)
  • Full resolution Color Grading in HDR mode
  • High-intensity Bloom with large scatter
  • Multiple local volumes blending at run-time
Optimized (recommended)
  • Conservative Bloom Intensity and Threshold
  • Global mild Color Grading, heavy effects reserved for cutscenes
  • Profile presets and lower sample counts for bloom if available
Practical test

Profile before and after enabling each effect. If frame time rises significantly, reduce quality or scope the effect to local volumes.

Key Takeaway

Measure and prioritize. Use subtle global adjustments and restrict expensive passes to where they contribute most to perceived quality.

screens.title: Hands-on Setup Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: Layer, Volume, Profile, and three basic effects

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through creating a working post-processing setup from scratch. First, verify you are using URP or HDRP and then open Window > Package Manager to install Post Processing. Next, add a new layer named PostProcessing in the Layers menu. Select the Main Camera, add the Post-Process Layer component, and set its layer mask to PostProcessing. Now create an empty GameObject named PostProcessGlobalVolume and assign it to the PostProcessing layer. Add a Post-Process Volume component and check Is Global. Create a Post-Process Profile asset in Assets > Create > Post-Process Profile and drag it into the Profile slot. With the profile selected, add Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading. Example starting values: Bloom Intensity 0.5 and Threshold 1.05; Vignette Intensity 0.3; Color Grading Temperature -10 and Contrast +15. Play the scene to observe changes and toggle each effect to see its contribution. Misconception: having a profile but no Post-Process Layer on the camera will show no effect. Final check: ensure the camera’s layer mask matches the volume’s GameObject layer. Your outcome should be a subtle, coherent mood change across the scene.

keyIdea.title: Step-by-step setup
keyIdea.text: Install package → create PostProcessing layer → add Post-Process Layer to camera → create global volume → create profile → add Bloom/Vignette/Color Grading.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity Setup Walkthrough

Step-by-step setup

Editor steps
  1. Ensure project uses URP or HDRP.
  2. Window > Package Manager > install Post Processing.
  3. Layers > Add Layer... > add "PostProcessing".
  4. Main Camera: Add Component > Post-Process Layer > set mask to PostProcessing.
  5. Create GameObject > Add Post-Process Volume > set to PostProcessing layer > check Is Global.
  6. Assets > Create > Post-Process Profile > drag to Profile slot.
  7. Add Bloom, Vignette, Color Grading and tune starting values.
Starting values to try
Bloom: Intensity = 0.5, Threshold = 1.05
Vignette: Intensity = 0.3
Color Grading: Temperature = -10, Contrast = +15
Play the scene and toggle each effect to compare. If nothing appears, recheck the camera’s Post-Process Layer and its layer mask.
Key Takeaway

Follow each editor step and validate by toggling effects. Consistent layering is the most common point of failure.

screens.title: Troubleshooting & Common Mistakes
screens.subtitle: Why effects don’t show and how to verify your setup

narration.text: When effects don’t appear there are a few common causes to check. First, confirm the Post-Process Layer is added to the camera and its Layer mask includes the layer assigned to your volume GameObject. Second, ensure the Post-Process Volume has a Profile assigned and that the effects within that profile have their Override checkbox enabled for the properties you expect to change. Third, check that Is Global is set appropriately for your intent; if you intended a global mood but left Is Global unchecked and placed the camera outside the bounds, the effects will not apply. Fourth, if you work outside URP/HDRP, verify compatibility—some behaviors differ and older stacks or alternatives may be required. A concrete validation sequence: toggle the Profile on and off while watching the Game view, use conservative test values so changes are visible, and move the camera into a local volume’s bounds to test blending. Misconceptions to avoid: assuming installation guarantees automatic application, or that effect values always look the same across exposures. The takeaway is a short checklist: camera layer mask, volume layer, profile assigned with overrides, and Is Global state. Resolve these in order to quickly restore expected behavior.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting checklist
keyIdea.text: Check camera Post-Process Layer mask, volume GameObject layer, profile assignments and overrides, and Is Global state when effects are missing.

content.html:
Troubleshooting Common Mistakes

Quick troubleshooting checklist

Checklist
  • Camera has Post-Process Layer and correct mask.
  • Volume GameObject is on the same layer as camera mask.
  • Profile asset is assigned and property overrides are enabled.
  • Is Global checked if you need scene-wide effects.
Validation steps
  1. Toggle the Profile on and off while watching the Game view.
  2. Move the camera into a local volume to test blending.
  3. Try minimal values so you can see subtle changes easily.
Misconception

Don’t assume post-processing will look identical across different exposure or device displays; always check target hardware.

Key Takeaway

Follow the checklist in order: camera mask, volume layer, profile overrides, and Is Global. These resolve most display issues quickly.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Post-Processing Essentials
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: These three key concepts summarize the most important ideas you should remember. First, post-processing runs after scene rendering and before display, and it’s used to shape mood and focus across the entire frame. Second, the Post-Process Layer on the camera and the Post-Process Volume in the scene must share a layer relationship so the camera knows which volumes to sample. Third, Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading are the core effects for mood: Bloom for glow, Vignette for focus, and Color Grading for palette and contrast. Each one interacts with exposure and each other, so tune them conservatively and validate on target hardware. Keep the checklist handy: install the package, add the camera layer, create a global volume and profile, and then add and tweak effects. These reminders will help you set up consistent, performant post-processing across your projects.

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Post-processing is a final global pass; camera layer mask plus volume layer connect the system; Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading shape mood.

content.html:
Key Concepts Remember
Post-Processing

A late full-screen pass that unifies lighting and sets mood across the frame.

Layer & Volume

Camera Post-Process Layer and Volume layer must match for effects to be applied.

Core Effects

Bloom, Vignette, Color Grading—use them conservatively and test interactions.

Takeaway

Install, wire camera and volume layers, then tune Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading with subtle, validated steps.

screens.title: Quick Reference Cards
screens.subtitle: Three one-line reminders for daily use

narration.text: Keep these three quick reference rules handy during your daily work. One: always confirm the Post-Process Layer is on the camera and its mask includes the volume layer. Two: use a global volume for scene-wide mood and reserve local volumes for transitions or region-specific looks. Three: tune Bloom, Vignette, and Color Grading in small steps and toggle changes to judge impact. Following these rules will greatly reduce setup errors and help you achieve consistent renders that look intentional across multiple scenes and target devices. Key Concepts Quick Reference
Camera mask

Ensure camera mask and volume layer match.

Volume scope

Use global for whole-scene, local for blended regions.

Conservative tuning

Adjust Bloom, Vignette, and Grading in small steps and test often.

Final Tip

Validate on the target platform and keep profiles organized for predictable results across scenes.
